definition: An integrated development environment, the program where you write, build and upload code all in one window.
A software development kit, the bundle of libraries, headers and tools you need to write programs for a particular device.
Software built into a device that runs its hardware, like VEXos on the V5 Brain, as opposed to the programs you upload.
A command-line interface, a program you control by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
A packaged, versioned bundle of library code that a PROS project can include, such as the PROS kernel itself.
A file of rules that tells the build tools which files to compile and how to combine them.
The core of an operating system. The PROS kernel is what starts your program and shares the processor among its tasks.
Sending a built program from your computer to the Brain, where it is stored in a program slot.
A file, usually ending in .h or .hpp, that tells the compiler what names exist so that other code can use them.
The place where a program starts running. In PROS, the kernel calls your functions, starting with initialize().
The set of functions in main.cpp that PROS calls as a match moves through its phases.
The part of a match when the robot runs from its program with no driver input.
The part of a match when drivers operate the robot with controllers.
A thing in your program that holds its own data and has actions you can ask it to do, like a motor.
A function that belongs to an object, called with a dot, as in intake.move(127).
A named group of code that keeps names from colliding, like the pros in pros::Motor.
One of the 21 numbered ports on the V5 Brain that connect to motors, radios and most sensors through a smart cable.
The setting in your code that says which cartridge a motor holds. Nothing checks it, so it has to match the real cartridge.
The removable gear unit inside a V5 motor that sets its top speed: 100, 200 or 600 RPM.
How hard electricity is being pushed through a circuit, measured in volts. A motor spins faster with more of it.
Revolutions per minute, a measure of how fast something spins.
Twisting force. A motor needs more of it to move a heavier or more stuck load.
A motor set up so that a positive command spins it the opposite way, marked in PROS with a negative port number.
What a motor does when told to stop: coast freely, brake, or actively hold its position.
The system at a competition that tells every robot when to be disabled, autonomous or under driver control.
A device that sends and receives data through the air instead of along a wire.
The radio module plugged into a Smart Port on the Brain, which links the robot to the controller.
Connecting a controller and a Brain so that they know to talk to each other wirelessly.
The name VEX gives its wireless system, which links a V5 controller to the radio on a V5 Brain.
One of the 8 numbered places on the Brain where an uploaded program is stored.
A text window on your computer that shows what a running program prints, and can send text back.
The delay between something being sent and it arriving.
A direct smart cable between the controller and the Brain, used to pair them and in place of the radio link.
A way of driving where each joystick controls the wheels on its own side of the robot.
A way of driving where one stick axis sets forward speed and another sets turning.
One direction of a stick's travel, reported as a number from -127 to 127.
A small range around a stick's center that the program treats as exactly zero, so a stick that doesn't quite center won't move the robot.
A function that reshapes stick input, usually to give finer control at low speeds.
Code that repeats on a steady schedule, reading inputs and updating outputs each time around.
The moment a signal changes from off to on, like the instant a button goes down.
Checking a value over and over on a schedule to notice when it changes.
Ignoring the very fast, false changes a physical switch can produce, so one press counts as one press.
A wheel with small rollers around its rim, so it grips going forward and slides easily sideways.
How fast an output is allowed to change. Limiting it keeps a motor command from jumping all at once.
A planned sequence of robot actions that runs with no driver.
Controlling something without measuring what actually happened.
Working out where you are from what you commanded or measured earlier, without checking against the outside world.
How closely a robot lands in the same place when it runs the same routine again.
A function call that doesn't return until its work is finished or its wait is over, so the next line has to wait.
A system that records the history of your files so you can compare, undo and share changes.
A project folder together with its full recorded history, often called a repo.
A saved snapshot of your project in Git's history, with a message saying what changed.
Choosing which changes will go into the next commit.
A view of exactly which lines changed between two versions.
A separate line of commits, so that you can try something without disturbing the working version.
Combining the changes from one branch into another.
What happens when two branches changed the same lines and Git needs a person to choose the result.
A copy of a repository hosted somewhere else, such as on GitHub.
Sending your commits to a remote.
Getting new commits from a remote and adding them to your copy.
Making your own full copy of a repository from a remote.
A file listing what Git should not track, such as build output.
